\chapter{Night}
\label{ch:ka-night}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} in Kannada and recognise it inside the midnight word I already knew.}

Say \kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ}, find it again inside \kn{ಮಧ್ಯರಾತ್ರಿ}, and note that native \kn{ಇರುಳು} lost its job where \kn{ಹಗಲು} kept a different one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ}]{\kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ} (rātri) — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} and its native cousin, pushed aside}

\label{lesson:KA-C24-ratri}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's \emph{dina} had a living native partner, \emph{hagalu}. This word's native partner tells a different, more honest story — one of being pushed out, not living alongside.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ}} (\textbf{rātri}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{} — is the same Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama} word already hiding inside \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯರಾತ್ರಿ}} (\emph{madhyarātri}, \textquotedblleft{}midnight,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 17), now standing on its own as Kannada's ordinary, everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}night.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Kannada \textbf{does} have a genuine \textbf{native Dravidian} word for night: \textbf{\kn{ಇರುಳು}} (\textbf{iruḷu}), from \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*cirVḷ}} — a real pan-Dravidian cognate, matching \textbf{Tamil}'s \textbf{\ta{இருள்}} (\emph{iruḷ}), \textbf{Malayalam}'s \textbf{\ml{ഇരുൾ}} (\emph{iruḷ}), and \textbf{Telugu}'s \textbf{\te{ఇరులు}} (\emph{irulu}). But here's the honest difference from last lesson's \emph{hagalu}: while \emph{hagalu} is still a \textbf{living, everyday} word (just for a different sense, \textquotedblleft{}daytime\textquotedblright{}), \emph{iruḷu} has been genuinely \textbf{pushed aside} by the Sanskrit loan — it now survives mainly in \textbf{older poetry}, carrying extra metaphorical weight (\textquotedblleft{}darkness,\textquotedblright{} even \textquotedblleft{}ignorance\textquotedblright{}), rather than in everyday speech. \emph{Rātri} simply \textbf{won} the job of \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} in modern Kannada.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rātri\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} already met inside madhyarātri
  \item \textquotedblleft{}iruḷu\textquotedblright{} — the real native word, now mostly archaic/poetic
  \item the honest contrast — hagalu still lives (different sense); iruḷu was pushed aside (same sense, lost the job)
\end{itemize}

(\textbf{Hagalu still lives}, for a different sense {[}\textquotedblleft{}daytime\textquotedblright{}{]}; \textbf{iruḷu was pushed aside} entirely by the Sanskrit loan, for the same sense {[}\textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}{]}.)
